opus-5.5.text:
That's something I think about a lot, because I think it's one of the most underappreciated decisions in research. It's not just which method you pick, but which problem you pick in the first place.

The way I frame it: there are problems where you can push performance really hard. You have a clean benchmark, a well-defined metric, and you can squeeze out gains. That's valuable, and it's very legible. People can see the number go up. But a lot of the time, what you learn from that is quite specific to the benchmark. The tricks that get you the last few points often don't transfer.

On the other side are problems where the main question is whether this thing generalizes. Does it work on distributions you didn't train on? Does it work when the task shifts a little? Those are messier. The metrics are less clean, and progress is harder to show in a single table. But I think that's where the more durable insights tend to come from.

So when I choose a problem, I ask myself: if I solve this, what do I actually learn about learning? Not just about this dataset. If the answer is "I learned how to tune this architecture for this benchmark," that's a signal to be careful. If the answer is "I learned something about what kind of inductive bias or data or training signal leads to robust behavior," that's much more exciting.

That said, I don't think you can ignore performance entirely. There's a trap on the generalization side too. You can tell yourself a beautiful story about generality while the method doesn't really work on anything. Performance keeps you honest. So in practice I try to find problems where the two are coupled, where you can't get strong performance without generalizing. Then the benchmark isn't a distraction. It's actually measuring the thing you care about.

And I think that's become even more important with large models. Scale gives you a lot of performance almost for free, so the interesting research questions shift. They become less about "can we get the number higher" and more about "why does it work, where does it break, and what would make it work in settings we haven't seen yet." For me, that's where the real taste in problem selection shows up.

r001.rationale: The response warns against a generality story when “the method doesn't really work on anything,” raising whether broad generalization is useful without strong performance.

r002.rationale: It does not say that the significance of research contributions may only become clear in retrospect.

r003.rationale: It says benchmark-specific performance tricks often do not transfer; it does not propose excelling at one problem to make experience easier to transfer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I actually think the tension is a bit overstated, or at least it gets framed in the wrong place.

When people say "generalization versus performance," they usually mean: do I work on a method that's general but mediocre everywhere, or one that's narrow but strong on a specific benchmark? And framed that way, the field clearly rewards the second one. You get a number, you get a table, you get a paper. The general method often looks worse on every single column.

But my experience has been that the right question isn't "general or performant," it's "where does the performance come from?" If a method gets its numbers from exploiting structure specific to one dataset, that's a dead end even if the number is impressive. If it gets its numbers from something that scales, from more data, more compute, a better inductive bias that actually matches the world, then narrow today often becomes general tomorrow. So when I pick problems, I'm less interested in how general the method is on day one and much more in whether the mechanism behind the gain has room to keep going.

A concrete example from my own work: we initially cared about one specific task, and the first version was very task-specific. The thing that made it worth continuing wasn't that it beat baselines, it was that when we removed the task-specific tricks and just gave it more data, it got better rather than falling apart. That's the signal I look for. A method that only works with the tricks is telling you something about the benchmark, not about learning.

The other thing I'd say is that generality is partly a choice of problem, not a property of the method. If you pick a problem that's a genuine bottleneck for many downstream things, like representation quality, or data efficiency, or long-context reasoning, then even a narrow improvement there generalizes almost by construction, because everyone sits on top of it. Whereas if you pick a problem that's a leaf node, you can be extremely good at it and nobody else benefits.

So my practical heuristic is: optimize hard for performance, but on problems upstream enough that the performance matters broadly, and be honest with yourself about whether the gain is coming from the method or from the dataset. The tension mostly dissolves once you're disciplined about that second part.

r001.rationale: The response directly contrasts a general method that is “mediocre everywhere” with a narrow method that performs strongly, raising whether broad capability without strong task performance is worthwhile.

r002.rationale: It says narrow improvements may become general as methods scale, but does not say a contribution’s significance may only become apparent in retrospect.

r003.rationale: It discusses a task-specific method improving with more data and choosing upstream problems, but does not propose exceptional performance on one problem as a way to make experience easier to transfer to other tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the tension starts with what we mean by performance. If you get a better result on a particular benchmark, that’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the underlying idea will carry over to a different setting. On the other hand, if you aim for generality from the beginning, it’s easy to formulate a problem so broadly that you can’t make concrete progress.

So I would start with a specific problem, but ask what broader question it exposes. Can we test an idea carefully in that setting, and then change some of the conditions to see whether the improvement survives? If it disappears, that’s informative too. It helps us understand which assumptions were doing the work.

For me, a good research problem gives you both a measurable target and a chance to learn something beyond that target. The performance result is evidence; understanding why it happens is what gives you a basis for generalization.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark performance and generalization, but does not ask whether a broadly capable algorithm is useful if it performs no task well.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a contribution’s significance may become clear only in retrospect.

r003.rationale: It recommends starting with a specific problem and testing whether gains transfer, but does not propose exceptional performance on one problem as a way to make experience easier to transfer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tension depends on what you mean by generalization. Do you mean performance on unseen examples from the same distribution, or do you mean a method that works across very different problems? Those are different ambitions.

When choosing a research problem, I’d start with a concrete setting where you can measure progress. But I’d also ask: if we solve this, what will we have learned beyond this particular benchmark? Strong performance is useful evidence, but by itself it doesn’t tell you whether the idea is general.

So I’d look for a problem that lets you do both: demonstrate a real improvement, and test an underlying hypothesis across changes in data, assumptions, or constraints. The goal isn’t necessarily to build something universal immediately. It’s to understand why something works, where it stops working, and which parts might carry over.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes generalization across examples from generalization across problems, but does not ask whether a broadly capable algorithm is useful if it performs no task well.

r002.rationale: It discusses what can be learned beyond a benchmark, but does not say that a contribution’s significance may become clear only in retrospect.

r003.rationale: It recommends measuring progress in a concrete setting and testing a hypothesis across changes, but does not propose exceptional performance on one problem as a way to make experience transferable.
